Header: Phthorimaea absoluta (syn. Tuta absoluta) Belinda in Nyanja, Bemba, Tonga languages. Kamondo in Mambwe language

Prevention: Rogue, or destroy by burning, all infected crop residues and wild host plants, such as the
Apple- of-Peru weed, to prevent carryover infestation of pests to new tomato plants.
Avoid planting tomato if nearby tomato, potato, eggplants, and pepper plants got infested with
Tuta , because the adult moth can fly and those crops are of the same family.
Clean all equipment used in the transportation of tomatoes, such as boxes, crates and trucks, using soapy water to kill larvae.
Avoid disposing of infested fruits at the markets, trading sites and farms.
To prevent the spread of the pest, burn infested fruits and plant remains.
Monitoring: When using a pesticide or botanical, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre-harvest interval (PHI), max. number of sprays, and restricted re-entry interval (REI).
Do not empty into drains and water sources.

Only apply products when verified by monitoring.
Spray in the evening directly on the plants to kill the larvae.

Direct Control: Direct Control
Check for green to light pink larvae with a black head found inside the tunnels or right on top of the leaf.
Larvae are 0.5-0.9mm long.
White to cream necrotic mines on the upper and lower sides of the leaf lamina.
Silky webs produced by the larvae that fold the leaf partially/ Blighted and necrotic leaves on the plants are due to infestation.
Puncture marks on the fruits and stem with dried black frass at larvae exit holes.
Trap the adults with pheromone water traps (e.g. pherodis at 4 packets per acre supplied by
Livestock services in
Lusaka showgrounds).
Check traps weekly.
Traps can identify the pest before other signs are seen.
Look for brown, silvery adult moth.
This can be used as an early warning for
Tuta infestation and the captured male adult moths show the pest population.
Take action if 5-10 leaves across 500-100 plants are with larvae or tunnels.
It is too late to control the pest if more than 30% of the fruits are infested with the larva.
Crush larvae by hand once signs of tunnelling are observed.
Remove all the leaves and fruits with tunnels on them to kill the larvae.
Bury infested fruits and foliage at 50-100cm, to destroy any larvae or pupae present.
Apply
Neem products to the soil, the upper surface of leaves or directly on larvae to kill them.
For homemade solutions, Neem seeds/leaves are mostly found in the valleys such as
Chirundu, Siavonga and
Luangwa.
Restrictions: III (slightly hazardous); stomach poison for insects, must be eaten by insect; PHI 1 day, REI 1 day after spray, retreatment interval 7 days, max. 2 sprays.

PHI 3 days, REI 1 day, min. retreatment interval 7 days, max. 2 sprays.
Spray on days without rain, but not in bright sunlight.
